opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say I underestimated it, at least on some dimensions, and overestimated it on others.

If you'd asked me a few years ago, I would have guessed that getting visually convincing, high-resolution, temporally coherent video, the kind where a casual viewer can't immediately tell it's generated, would take quite a bit longer. The jump in visual fidelity came much faster than I expected. Scaling worked. Better data curation, diffusion and transformer architectures, and simply more compute pushed the "it looks real" frontier forward remarkably quickly.

Where I was too optimistic, or at least where the field still has a long way to go, is the deeper part: physical consistency and controllability. Coming from robotics, that's what I care about most. A video can look beautiful frame by frame, but if a cup passes through a hand, or an object's mass and momentum don't make sense, or a door's state changes for no reason when the camera turns back, the model hasn't really understood the world. It has learned appearance, not dynamics. I had hoped video models would pick up intuitive physics as a byproduct of scale, and they have to some extent, more than skeptics predicted. But it's patchy. Contact-rich interactions, long-horizon consistency, and precise response to actions are still hard.

So my current view is that video generation is progressing on two clocks. On the content-creation clock, things are moving extremely fast, and the remaining gaps are length, editing control, and cost. On the world-model clock, using these models as simulators where an agent or a robot can take an action and get a faithful prediction of what happens next, we're earlier than the demos suggest. That's the one I find most exciting. If we get there, it changes how we train embodied intelligence, because you could learn from a learned simulator instead of collecting everything on real hardware.

My expectation now is that the next few years will be less about prettier pixels and more about action conditioning, interactivity, and physical grounding. I've learned to be humble about timelines, though. In this field, the things you think are five years away sometimes show up in eighteen months, and the things you think are close turn out to hide very deep problems.

r001.rationale: The response says, “I underestimated it,” and explains that visual fidelity advanced faster than expected.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I was too conservative. When we started on video generation, I remember thinking it would take maybe three to five years before we got something that was genuinely usable, not just a research demo. The physics looked so hard. Temporal consistency, object permanence, lighting that stays coherent across frames. I thought each of those would be its own multi-year problem.

And then Sora came out, and within a year you had a handful of teams producing results that would have seemed impossible to me two years earlier. So my timelines were off by a factor of maybe two or three.

What I underestimated was how much the same recipe transfers. I kept thinking video needed fundamentally new ideas. In reality, a lot of it was the same lesson as language models: scale the data, scale the compute, use a clean architecture, and many of the problems you thought required special handling just start to dissolve. The model learns something about physics implicitly because it has seen enough of the world.

What I overestimated, on the other hand, is how fast it would become useful in production. The demos moved faster than I expected, but the gap between a beautiful ten-second clip and something a filmmaker or an advertiser can actually control, iterate on, and trust is still large. Controllability, consistency across shots, cost per generation. Those are moving slower than the raw quality did.

So if I had to summarize, I was wrong on the capability curve, in the direction of being too pessimistic. And I was probably a bit too optimistic about how quickly capability turns into adoption. Both of those are lessons I try to carry into how I think about the next phase, especially for world models and robotics, where I suspect the same pattern will repeat.

r001.rationale: The response says, “I was too conservative” and that the timelines were off by a factor of two or three, clearly indicating Jie Tan underestimated the pace of video generation’s development.

astra-6.text: Looking back, I think I underestimated how quickly video generation would progress. I expected improvements to come more gradually, but the gains in visual quality and consistency have moved faster than I anticipated. At the same time, generating an impressive clip is different from making a tool that reliably produces exactly what you want. So I’d separate those two things: I’m more optimistic about the pace of the underlying technology, while still cautious about how quickly it becomes dependable in everyday production.

r001.rationale: The candidate says, “I underestimated how quickly video generation would progress,” directly stating that Jie Tan underestimated its pace.

sol-6.1.text: I think I underestimated how quickly it would develop. My earlier expectations were more conservative, especially about how soon video generation would produce results that feel coherent and useful. Looking back, I’d revise that timeline forward. But I’d still distinguish between an impressive short clip and a system that reliably gives you the exact video you want. The progress has been faster than I expected; achieving consistent control is a separate challenge.
